title: The Hippopotamus and Crocodile Hunt (Jagd auf Nilpferd und Krokodil)

work.text: Rubens contributed to the long-standing genre of the large hunting scene and his studio produced dozens for aristocratic patrons in the 1610s and 1620s.

In treating subjects of this character, Rubens found how thoroughly they suited his temperament. Judging by the number of variants that he painted himself, or caused to be painted in his studio, they must have found favour with the public.

source.author: Émile Michel
source.title: Rubens: His Life, His Work, and His Time, vol. 1, trans. Elizabeth Lee

moment.text: The accurately rendered physical appearances of the hippopotamus and crocodile contrast with contemporary renderings and reflect the period's growing interest in empiricism and natural history. It has been suggested that Rubens may have traveled to Rome to view a temporarily displayed dead hippopotamus preserved in brine prior to the painting of the picture.
Delacroix greatly admired this work. … “which is more ferocious, and of which he liked the emphasis, and the relaxed, extravagant forms.”

source.author: Émile Michel
source.title: Rubens: His Life, His Work, and His Time, vol. 1, trans. Elizabeth Lee

matters.text: Maximilian I, Elector of Bavaria, commissioned the Hippopotamus and Crocodile Hunt three others depicting lion, wolf, and boar hunts, in 1615 to decorate Schleißheim Palace, the summer residence of the Wittelsbach princes.
I am so overwhelmed with works and commissions, both public and private, that for some years I cannot dispose of myself

source.author: Peter Paul Rubens
source.title: Letter to Sir Dudley Carleton, April 1618, in W. Noël Sainsbury, Original Unpublished Papers Illustrative of the Life of Sir Peter Paul Rubens
